facts.title: Born From a Single Atom
facts.text: Meitnerium was first created on 29 August 1982 at the GSI Helmholtz Centre in Darmstadt, Germany, by a team led by Peter Armbruster and Gottfried Münzenberg. They detected just one single atom, produced by firing iron-58 ions at a bismuth-209 target in the SHIP velocity filter. Confirming a brand-new element from one atom required meticulous tracking of its radioactive decay chain.

facts.title: Named for a Pioneer Physicist
facts.text: The element honors Lise Meitner (1878-1968), the Austrian-Swedish physicist who, with Otto Frisch, provided the theoretical explanation for nuclear fission. Although her collaborator Otto Hahn won the 1944 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for the discovery, Meitner was controversially overlooked. Meitnerium is one of the few elements named after a woman, alongside curium (partly for Marie Curie).

facts.title: A Synthetic Element, Never Found in Nature
facts.text: Meitnerium does not occur naturally anywhere on Earth or, as far as we know, in the cosmos. Every atom that has ever existed was deliberately manufactured in a particle accelerator. This is because all its isotopes are intensely radioactive and decay far too quickly to have survived since the elements formed in stars and supernovae.

facts.title: Gone in the Blink of an Eye
facts.text: All known isotopes of meitnerium are extremely unstable, with very short half-lives. The longest-lived isotope identified so far, meitnerium-278, has a half-life of only about 4 to 8 seconds. Most others vanish in fractions of a second, decaying mainly through alpha emission or spontaneous fission.

facts.title: A Member of Group 9
facts.text: On the periodic table meitnerium sits in group 9, directly below cobalt, rhodium, and iridium, making it a transition metal. Chemists predict it should behave somewhat like iridium, possibly favoring a +3 or +1 oxidation state. However, these properties remain theoretical because no one has ever assembled enough atoms to study its chemistry directly.

facts.title: Probably a Dense, Heavy Metal
facts.text: Theoretical calculations suggest meitnerium would be a solid metal at room temperature with an extraordinarily high density, estimated at roughly 27-28 grams per cubic centimeter. That would make it one of the densest substances ever, rivaling or exceeding osmium and iridium. Because samples never exist in bulk, this density has only been predicted, never weighed.

facts.title: Relativity Reshapes Its Atoms
facts.text: In superheavy elements like meitnerium, the innermost electrons move at a substantial fraction of the speed of light. This triggers relativistic effects that contract some electron orbitals and expand others, subtly altering the element's predicted chemistry. Scientists study meitnerium precisely to test whether Einstein's relativity bends the rules of the periodic table at its extreme edge.

facts.title: Cooked Up by Cold Fusion
facts.text: The original synthesis used a technique called cold fusion, which here means fusing two medium-weight nuclei gently enough that the merged nucleus survives rather than instantly flying apart. Iron-58 striking bismuth-209 produced meitnerium-266 plus a single neutron. This careful, low-energy approach was pioneered at GSI and helped create several other superheavy elements.

facts.title: A Name That Took 15 Years
facts.text: Although GSI proposed the name meitnerium soon after the 1982 discovery, the International Union of Pure and Applied Chemistry did not officially approve it until 1997. During the interim it carried the placeholder systematic name unnilennium, symbol Une, simply meaning one-zero-nine in Latin-Greek roots. Such delays were common amid disputes over who deserved credit for the heaviest elements.

facts.title: Purely a Research Curiosity
facts.text: Meitnerium has no commercial, industrial, medical, or biological uses whatsoever, and it plays no role in any living organism. Its sole value is scientific: it helps researchers map the limits of nuclear stability and search for the theorized island of stability, where some superheavy nuclei might last much longer. Studying it deepens our understanding of how matter behaves at the frontier of the periodic table.
